summary: Describes a way to save IP address space by letting hosts inside an enterprise use addresses that are not globally unique, while still allowing connectivity within the enterprise and among public hosts. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 1918.

plainLanguage.summary: Houses on different streets can share house numbers if the numbers only matter inside each street. This lets companies reuse addresses inside. A newer note replaced it.

questions: which ip addresses can i use internally
subtitle: Using non-unique IP addresses inside enterprises to conserve address space

tldr.problem: The finite supply of globally unique IPv4 addresses would be exhausted quickly if every computer in every enterprise needed a unique address, even those that never connect to the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: This document reserves three ranges of IP addresses for private use within enterprises: 10.0.0.0-10.255.255.255, 172.16.0.0-172.31.255.255, and 192.168.0.0-192.168.255.255. These addresses are not routable on the public Internet.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 1918, which codifies the same practice, but enabled enterprises to save vast amounts of global address space.

facts.label: Key constraint
facts.value: Routing info about private networks must not be forwarded to the Internet

today: RFC 1918 obsoletes this document. RFC 1918 codifies the same three private address blocks and practices, and has become the standard reference for private IPv4 addressing.

sections.title: The Address Shortage Problem
sections.content:
The Internet originally allocated IP addresses assuming every computer would eventually need a globally unique address to connect to the public Internet. But many devices inside companies never need external connectivity: they are internal workstations, cash registers, parking lot displays, or equipment behind firewalls.

The RFC identifies three types of hosts: those that never need external connectivity, those that need limited external access (through application-layer gateways like email or FTP), and those that need full Internet connectivity. Only the third category truly requires globally unique addresses. By allowing the first two categories to use non-unique, locally meaningful addresses, enterprises could dramatically reduce their consumption of the global address pool.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every computer inside a bank needs to be reachable from the Internet. Many computers just talk to other computers inside the bank. If they all used fake addresses that only work internally, we'd save real addresses for computers that need them.

sections.title: The Private Address Blocks
sections.content:
IANA reserved three blocks of IP addresses for private use: the 24-bit block (10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255), which is a single Class A network with 16 million addresses; the 20-bit block (172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255), which is 16 contiguous Class B networks with about 1 million addresses; and the 16-bit block (192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255), which is 256 contiguous Class C networks with about 65,000 addresses.

These addresses are non-unique globally: many enterprises can use the same private addresses simultaneously. An enterprise using private addresses does not need IANA approval. However, enterprises still need globally unique addresses for any hosts that require external connectivity. The key constraint is that routers on the Internet boundary should filter out routing information about private networks, preventing private addresses from leaking into the global routing system.
sections.plainLanguage: Three ranges of addresses are reserved for private use. 10.0.0.0 is huge, 172.16.0.0 is medium, and 192.168.0.0 is smaller. Any company can use any of these without asking permission.

sections.title: Deploying Private Addresses
sections.content:
Enterprises should design their network by first mapping out all internal connectivity needs and using private addresses everywhere internally, then adding public addresses at the edge where external connectivity is needed. This preserves the largest contiguous blocks of private space for future growth.

When a host must change from private to public status (or vice versa), its address must change, which requires renumbering. The RFC recommends designing subnets so that hosts likely to undergo such changes in the future are grouped together, minimizing disruption. Routers at the enterprise boundary should be configured with filters to prevent private addresses and routing information about private networks from escaping. Many enterprises use Network Address Translation (NAT) to translate between private internal addresses and a few public external addresses, though NAT is not explicitly discussed in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Design the inside of the company first using private addresses. At the edge, translate to real addresses. If a computer needs to become external later, it needs a new address.

sections.title: Benefits and Tradeoffs
sections.content:
The primary benefit is conservation of globally unique address space, which directly extends the lifetime of the IPv4 address pool. Enterprises also gain flexibility: they have much more address space to work with, allowing for cleaner address plans and easier network growth. The RFC notes that for enterprises that have used addresses before connecting to the Internet, private addresses provide a safe way to avoid collisions with addresses already assigned to other organizations.

The main drawback is that moving a host between private and public status requires renumbering, which is inconvenient. However, the RFC argues this is not as severe as it may seem: many hosts may never move, and tools like DHCP (mentioned as an emerging technology) can automate renumbering. Moreover, the RFC notes that even hosts with globally unique addresses may need renumbering as enterprises change Internet service providers, so the renumbering concern is not unique to private addressing.
sections.plainLanguage: The benefit is saving millions of addresses. The downside is if a computer needs to become public later, it must change addresses. But many computers never need to change.

sections.title: Operational Best Practices
sections.content:
The RFC recommends several operational practices. Routers connecting enterprises to external networks should use packet and routing filters at both ends to prevent leakage of private addresses. Enterprises should filter inbound routing information about private networks to avoid being confused by ambiguous routing. Two-nameserver DNS configurations are recommended: one external server for public addresses (linked into global DNS) and one internal server for all addresses (both public and private), preventing information about private hosts from leaking beyond the enterprise.

For enterprises using external connectivity, the RFC suggests using IP tunnels between sites to prevent private addresses from leaking when connections cross external networks. The clear separation of public and private addresses, while requiring renumbering when status changes, also makes uncontrolled external connectivity more difficult, providing a security benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: Set up walls around your private network so private addresses don't escape to the Internet. Run two separate DNS servers so outsiders only see public addresses.
